title: Tables, rows and SELECT
summary: Meet the Data Desk, the bookshop's database, and your first query.

steps.title: Welcome to the Data Desk
body: You have just joined **Larkspur Holdings**, a family of odd little businesses in the harbour city of Port Avalon: a bookshop, a bike-share, a hospital, a game studio. Every one of them runs on a database, and every one of them has questions nobody can answer.

Rosa Quint, the chief analyst, slides a laptop across the desk. *"Your first client is Inkwell & Ivy, the bookshop downstairs. Learn to ask their database questions and the rest of the city opens up."*
A **relational database** stores data in **tables**. A table is a grid:
- Each **column** is one fact about every thing (its title, its price).
- The **primary key** (`id`) is a column whose value is unique per row, so every row can be pointed at.
**SQL** (Structured Query Language) is how you ask a database questions. You say *what* you want; the database works out *how* to get it.

steps.prompt: In the `books` table, what is **one row**?
options: Everything the shop knows about one particular book
One fact, such as a price, for every book
steps.explain: A row is one record (one book). A column is one fact across every record, like all the titles.

steps.title: SELECT ... FROM
body: A query starts with `SELECT` (which columns) and `FROM` (which table):
- List columns with commas. `SELECT *` means *every column*.
- Keywords are case-insensitive (`select` works), but writing them in capitals makes queries easy to scan.
- Line breaks don't matter. The `;` ends the statement.
- `SELECT` can also compute without a table at all: `SELECT 2 + 2;` returns `4`.
> **Tip:** Rows come back in **no promised order** unless you ask for one. You will learn `ORDER BY` next lesson.

steps.prompt: SELECT doesn't need a table. What does this return? (Separate columns with ` | `.)
steps.explain: Each expression after `SELECT` becomes a column. Text values go in **single quotes** in SQL.

steps.title: Shelf labels
prompt: The bookshop wants shelf labels. Return the **title** and **author** of every book.
Table: `books(id, title, author, genre, price, pages, year, stock)`
setup: CREATE TABLE books (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, author TEXT, genre TEXT, price REAL, pages INTEGER, year INTEGER, stock INTEGER);

steps.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a grid of rows and columns about one kind of thing
one record, such as one customer
one named fact stored for every record
a column whose value identifies exactly one row

steps.prompt: Complete the query so it returns every customer's name and email.
steps.explain: `SELECT` the columns, `FROM` the table, `;` to finish.

steps.title: Meet the customers
prompt: Rosa wants to see the whole customer list with every column, exactly as stored.
setup: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT, email TEXT, points INTEGER);

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Ana Sousa','Port Avalon','ana@mail.test',120),(2,'Ben Okoro','Kestrel Bay',NULL,40),(3,'Chloe Park','Port Avalon','chloe@mail.test',NULL),(4,'Dmitri Volkov','Elmsworth','dmitri@mail.test',300),(5,'Esme Hart','Kestrel Bay','esme@mail.test',0),(6,'Farid Nasser','Port Avalon',NULL,75),(7,'Greta Lund',NULL,'greta@mail.test',15);
hints: There is a shortcut for *every column*.

steps.prompt: You run `SELECT name FROM customers;` twice. Which statement is true?
options: The rows might come back in a different order, because no order was asked for
The rows always come back sorted by name
The rows always come back in the order they were inserted
The query fails because there is no WHERE clause
steps.explain: Without `ORDER BY`, SQL promises the rows but not their order. Small tables often *look* ordered, which is exactly why this catches people out.

prompt: For tonight's stock take, return each book's **title**, **stock** and **price**, in that column order.
